name: Upanishads
info: The Upanishads are Sanskrit texts of the late Vedic and post-Vedic periods, composed in northern India and the most recent addition to the Vedas; the oldest are placed in the 7th to 6th centuries BCE.

facts.made: Mostly anonymous; teachings are attributed to sages such as Yajnavalkya, Uddalaka Aruni and Shvetaketu, and the Shvetashvatara names its own author; scholars regard the existing texts as the work of many authors
facts.form: Sanskrit texts, in prose and verse; 108 are listed in the Muktika canon, of which the first dozen or so, the mukhya (principal) Upanishads, are the oldest
facts.where: Embedded in the Brahmanas and Aranyakas of the four Vedas; manuscripts of the 108 with Brahma-Yogin's commentary are held at the Adyar Library
facts.known: Atman and Brahman; the doctrine of karma; moksha (liberation); one of the earliest declarations of ahimsa; the Mahavakyas such as Tat tvam asi; a basis for the schools of Vedanta; Persian, Latin and English translations

t: The Upanishads are the latest layer of the Vedas and turn from ritual toward questions of the self (Atman) and ultimate reality (Brahman).
They hold a plurality of ideas: some are described as monistic, others, such as the Katha, as dualistic, and later Vedanta schools read them in divergent ways.
Scholars give only broad dates, from about 800 to 300 BCE for the principal texts, and new texts called Upanishads went on being composed into the early modern era.
dyk: In 1656 Dara Shukoh produced the Sirr-i-Akbar, a Persian translation of 50 Upanishads; a Latin version made from a Persian manuscript was published in 1801 and 1802, and Schopenhauer kept a copy by his side.
ev: Olivelle places the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya Upanishads, the two earliest, in these centuries, give or take a century or so
The prose Upanishads Taittiriya, Aitareya and Kausitaki follow, in Olivelle's chronology
Badarayana's Brahmasutra synthesises the differing accounts of Atman and Brahman
Shankara develops the Advaita ideas of Gaudapada and comments on 11 mukhya Upanishads
Dara Shukoh's Sirr-i-Akbar translates 50 Upanishads from Sanskrit into Persian
Anquetil-Duperron publishes his Latin translation, Oupnek'hat, in two volumes (1801 to 1802)
Max Müller's first volume begins the first systematic English treatment of the 12 principal Upanishads
Yeats and Shri Purohit Swami publish The Ten Principal Upanishads

sections.origins:
The Upanishads are Sanskrit texts of the late Vedic and post-Vedic periods. They are described as documenting “the transition from the archaic ritualism of the Veda into new religious ideas and institutions”, and they are the most recent addition to the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism. Earlier parts of the Vedas dealt with mantras, benedictions, rituals, ceremonies and sacrifices.

The mukhya Upanishads are found mostly in the concluding part of the Brahmanas and Aranyakas. They were memorised by each generation for centuries and passed down orally. Scholars regard northern India as the general area of composition for the early texts: a region bounded on the west by the upper Indus valley, on the east by the lower Ganges region, on the north by the Himalayan foothills and on the south by the Vindhya range.

Scholars are reasonably sure the early Upanishads arose in Kuru-Panchala and Kosala-Videha, a “frontier region” of Brahmanism, together with areas to the south and west. Witzel identifies the Brihadaranyaka's centre of activity as Videha, whose king Janaka features prominently in it. Attempts to place individual texts are still tentative.
sections.content:
The central concern of all the Upanishads is to discover the relations between ritual, cosmic realities, including the gods, and the human body or person. They postulate Atman (self) and Brahman as the “summit of the hierarchically arranged and interconnected universe”, though various ideas about how the two relate can be found. Older texts state that Atman is part of Brahman but not identical, while younger ones state that they are identical.

The texts reflect a pluralism of worldviews. Some are deemed monistic; others, including the Katha, are dualistic, and the Maitri inclines toward the dualism that grounded the Samkhya and Yoga schools. The Chandogya includes one of the earliest known declarations of ahimsa (non-violence) as an ethical precept, and the Brihadaranyaka presents the doctrine of karma. Knowledge of Atman is called vidya, true knowledge, while knowledge of Maya, the changing world, is avidya.

The older Upanishads attack ritual with increasing intensity. The Chandogya compares those who perform sacrifices to a procession of dogs chanting “Om! Let's eat. Om! Let's drink.” The Brihadaranyaka reads the horse sacrifice, ashvamedha, allegorically. Vedic gods such as Agni, Indra and Vishnu are equated with the Brahman-Atman, and self-realisation becomes the means to moksha, liberation.
sections.making:
The authorship of most Upanishads is unknown. Radhakrishnan notes that almost all early Indian literature was anonymous. Some traditionally consider the Vedas apauruseya, “not of a man”, while the Vedic texts themselves assert that they were skilfully created by Rishis, or sages, as a carpenter builds a chariot. The early teachings are attributed to sages such as Yajnavalkya, Uddalaka Aruni, Shvetaketu, Shandilya, Aitareya, Balaki, Pippalada and Sanatkumara, and women such as Maitreyi and Gargi take part in the dialogues. The Shvetashvatara closes with credits to a sage of that name, who is considered its author.

Many scholars believe the early texts were interpolated and expanded over time. Manuscripts of the same Upanishad found in different parts of South Asia differ, as do the surviving non-Sanskrit versions, and each text varies in metre, style, grammar and structure. The existing texts are believed to be the work of many authors.

Dating rests on scanty evidence. Patrick Olivelle says any dating closer than a few centuries is “as stable as a house of cards”. He places the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya in the 7th to 6th centuries BCE and the verse texts, beginning with the Kena, in the last few centuries BCE. Gavin Flood gives about 600 to 300 BCE, Stephen Phillips 800 to 300 BCE, and Johannes Bronkhorst argues for a later date, possibly close to the grammarians Katyayana and Patanjali, around the 2nd century BCE.
sections.reception:
The Upanishads form one of the three main sources of all schools of Vedanta, with the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahmasutra, together called the Prasthanatrayi. Because of the variety of teachings in them, several interpretations could be grounded on them. Advaita holds there is no difference between Atman and Brahman; Vishishtadvaita sees the individual soul as part of Brahman, similar but not identical; Dvaita treats souls and matter as eternal and separate entities. Shankara, the 8th-century figure of Advaita, commented on 11 mukhya Upanishads and drew four Mahavakyas, great sayings, from them, including “Tat tvam asi” (“That Thou art”) from the Chandogya.

Ramanuja (1017 to 1137 CE) and Madhvacharya (1199 to 1278 CE) each held that his own school was grounded in the Upanishads. Scholars differ on Shankara: King suggests many of his ideas are at odds with the Upanishads, while Radhakrishnan sees them as straightforward developments.

The Upanishads also attracted comment on their relation to Buddhism and to the philosophy of Pythagoras and Plato. Jayatilleke contrasts the Upanishadic assumption of an Atman with the Buddhist finding that none exists. Some scholars have seen parallels with Pythagoras and Plato; others, such as Keith, Burnet and Wadia, think the systems developed independently, noting there is no historical evidence of the philosophers meeting.
sections.survival:
Texts of the Upanishads were long kept orally. In the modern era the ancient Upanishads, embedded in the Brahmana and Aranyaka layers of the Vedas, were detached, compiled into separate texts and gathered into anthologies, each list associating a text with one of the four Vedas. The lists are inconsistent. In south India a list of 108 based on the Muktika Upanishad, published in Telugu, was the most common by the 19th century, while in north India a list of 52 has been most common.

The Muktika Upanishad, which predates 1656 CE, lists 108 canonical Upanishads, including itself last, and groups the first 13 as mukhya. There is no fixed list beyond it. More than 200 Upanishads are known, and in 1908 Friedrich Schrader named four newly found ones Bashkala, Chhagaleya, Arsheya and Saunaka; three were incomplete and inconsistent, likely poorly maintained or corrupted.

Sectarian Upanishads, such as those of Shaktism, Shaivism and Vaishnavism, were composed through to about 1600 CE. Such texts do not enjoy status as shruti, and the authority of the new Upanishads as scripture is not accepted in Hinduism. Manuscripts of the 108 with Brahma-Yogin's commentary are held at the Adyar Library.
sections.legacy:
The Mughal emperor Akbar's reign saw the first translations into Persian, and in 1656 his great-grandson Dara Shukoh produced the Sirr-i-Akbar with 50 Upanishads. Anquetil-Duperron put the Persian into Latin, published in 1801 and 1802, and this introduced the Upanishads to Western scholars, although Deussen held that the Persian translators took great liberties. Colebrooke made the first Sanskrit-to-English translation, of the Aitareya, in 1805, and Rammohun Roy the first English Kena in 1816. Max Müller's editions of 1879 and 1884 were the first systematic English treatment of the 12 principal texts. Later translators include Hume, Deussen, Radhakrishnan and Olivelle, whose work won the 1998 A.K. Ramanujan Book Prize.

Schopenhauer read the Latin version and praised the Upanishads in The World as Will and Representation (1819) and Parerga and Paralipomena (1851); Schelling praised them too, and the American transcendentalists, among them Emerson and Thoreau, were influenced. Erwin Schrödinger wrote that the unity of minds is “the doctrine of the Upanishads”. T. S. Eliot based the final portion of The Waste Land (1922) on one of the verses, and the Upanishads were among the few books Gustav Holst kept for his whole life. Yeats and Shri Purohit Swami published The Ten Principal Upanishads in 1938.

summary: The Upanishads are Sanskrit texts of the late Vedic period, the latest layer of the Vedas, which turn from ritual to questions about the self, Atman, and ultimate reality, Brahman. Mostly anonymous, they are dated only broadly and have been read in many ways by the schools of Vedanta.
references: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upanisads (Oxford University Press, 1998)
Paul Deussen, The philosophy of the Upanishads (T. & T. Clark, 1908)
Arthur Berriedale Keith, The Religion and Philosophy of the Veda and Upanishads (Motilal Banarsidass Publishers, 2007)
R. D. Ranade, A constructive survey of Upanishadic philosophy (Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan, 1926)
notes: Start year -700 is Olivelle's 7th to 6th centuries BCE for Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya; Phillips gives 800 to 300 BCE, Flood 600 to 300 BCE, Bronkhorst later (c. 2nd century BCE).
The article says both 'more than 200 known Upanishads' and 'new Upanishads number in the hundreds'; I used 'more than 200'.

Article gives the Muktika canon's span as last centuries of the 1st millennium BCE to about the 15th century CE in the lead, but new Upanishads 'through the early modern era (~1600 CE)'; I used about 1600 CE for sectarian ones.
Left out: Platonic details, Mascaro and Easwaran, Maya beyond vidya/avidya, the table of 108 (absent from saved text).
Article is thin on manuscripts: no oldest manuscript date is given.
